newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis see India's Gujral pursuing dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis see India's Gujral pursuing dialogue.

text.p: The choice of Inder Kumar Gujral as India's new prime minister bodes well for a fledgling dialogue with Islamabad, but may not lead to swift progress in the talks, Pakistani officials and analysts said on Sunday.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's press and information adviser Mushahid Hussain said Pakistan would welcome Gujral as prime minister, recalling a "cordial and pleasant" meeting between Gujral and Sharif, then in opposition, in 1995.

"We would look forward to renewing that relationship and also hope that Mr Gujral, as he was stating when he was not in the government in the past, would take steps to resolve the primary cause of friction between India and Pakistan, namely the the unresolved dispute of Jammu and Kashmir," he told Reuters.
In New Delhi, Gujral said on Sunday he would continue to try to improve relations with India's South Asian neighbours.

"As foreign minister, I have built some sort of a doctrine regarding neighbourly relations. That will continue to be my priority area," said Gujral, who was foreign minister in the outgoing government of caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
His United Front coalition, whose parliamentarians chose him as their leader on Saturday, said President Shankar Dayal Sharma was likely to ask Gujral to form a government later on Sunday.

Hussain said Gujral "comes across as a person with a positive perspective on relations with Pakistan and we only hope that in his new position he will be able to translate that perspective into a practical policy".
He said Gujral's appointment would improve the ambience of India-Pakistan relations, but Islamabad was aware of forces in India that might constrain his ability to make a major move.

"We only hope the Indian leadership and the new prime minister, who has been an advocate of better relations with Pakistan,...would be able to translate that vision into reality, notwithstanding the constraints inherent in India's political instability at the moment," he said.
A senior Foreign Ministry official praised Gujral's "understanding of the problems of the region".

The official, who asked not to be identified, said Gujral had in the past been active in so-called Track 2 diplomacy involving non-governmental contacts between Indians and Pakistanis keen to promote peace between the rival neighbours.
"We would very much want him to transfer his Track 2 skills to Track 1," said the official.

"Now that he is prime minister he is in an ideal position to seize this historic opportunity we have to solve our problems, particularly Jammu and Kashmir, and to free South Asia from tension so that we can both get on with economic development."
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain 50 years ago, two of them over Kashmir.
Top Pakistani and Indian diplomats met for three days in New Delhi at the end of March, the first such talks since 1994.

Gujral, as foreign minister, met his Pakistani counterpart Gohar Ayub at a Non-Aligned Movement conference in Delhi this month. More talks between foreign ministry officials may take place in Islamabad before a possible meeting between the two prime ministers at a regional summit in the Maldives in May.
Pakistani analysts said Gujral would pursue the talks, but there was no certainty that they would produce results.

"Given that he is the architect of this process, I would imagine this is almost a guarantee that...he will make a special effort for them to be sustained," said Maleeha Lodhi, former ambassador to the United States. "But whether this means any substantive movement, I really have my doubts."
Syed Talat Hussain, who writes for the daily newspaper The News, said India's three-week political crisis had cast a cloud of uncertainty over the dialogue with Pakistan.
Gujral's emergence as head of the United Front to lead a centre-left government with the support of the Congress Party augured better for the talks than other possible scenarios.
But he said no early breakthrough should be expected at a time when Indian politicians were preoccupied with stabilising the country's internal political situation.
"They have an immediate political crisis on their hands and they want to resolve that permanently before they move on to talking to Pakistan, which itself is politically explosive."
